007-ice-racer.title: 007 Ice Racer
007-ice-racer.summary: James Bond’s Vanquish races through four missions inspired by Die Another Day.

sections.heading: The game
sections.text: Drive the Vanquish past obstacles and collect extra time, points and speed. One mission replaces the race against the clock with a fight against Zao, using rockets picked up on the road.

sections.heading: Development
sections.text: Marc Pestka designed the game and its levels. Programming was shared by Benoit Laffitte, Jérôme Schurch and Eric Thommerot; Schurch also produced it.

sections.heading: Release and reception
sections.text: The Q Store offered optional power-ups paid for by SMS. DJcube revisited the ExEn game in 2023 and completed its four missions in about six minutes.

platform.heading: The platform
platform.text: ExEn stood for Execution Engine. In-Fusio built the game platform into compatible handsets; players downloaded games over the air and ran them locally. Panasonic’s European GD67 launch in September 2002 included ExEn 2.0, with colour and 3D support.

platform.heading: Tools and distribution
platform.text: In August 2002, In-Fusio opened a Developer Zone with design guidance, technical FAQs and a forum. An SDK download was announced as forthcoming. The company also offered revenue sharing and a fast-track deployment programme for original game concepts.

platform.heading: Working at In-Fusio
platform.text: Arnaud Storq, known as NoRecess, joined In-Fusio in Bordeaux around 2000. In his 2024 conversation with Dr JVtek, he recalled making small arcade games and an isometric adventure on 16 MHz hardware, with tiny monochrome displays in several resolutions.

quotes.text: I have never seen as much QA as in that period
quotes.speaker: Arnaud Storq / NoRecess
quotes.translation: From the edited English transcript published by NoRecess.

platform.heading: Testing on a phone
platform.text: Storq remembered a large test team. A game crash could affect the handset itself, leaving the operator and phone manufacturer with a problem as well as the game company. His recollection concerns the early platform he worked on.

platform.heading: A proposed mobile game API
platform.text: In-Fusio submitted JSR 178, a proposed Mobile Game API for resource-limited Java devices. Thomas Landspurg was specification lead and Frederic Condolo the contact. The proposal covered sprites, graphics, collision handling, multiplayer facilities and 3D. The Java Community Process rejected it; it did not become an adopted standard.
